body.text: North Korea has been issuing in rapid succession statements being attributed to Kim Yo Jong, Director of General Affairs of the Central Committee of the Workers’ Party of Korea and younger sister of supreme leader Kim Jong Un. In August, she criticized Japan’s defense buildup, while in September she condemned the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) denuclearization demands on North Korea and denounced U.S.-led multilateral military exercises. Kim also pushed back against South Korea’s account of a landmine explosion incident near the inter-Korean military demarcation line, and in October she unleashed a torrent of condemnation directed at South Korea’s plan to provide medical equipment. Kim Yo Jong has become a channel through which North Korea issues messages on a wide range of topics directed at Japan, the United States, and South Korea.

The first statement under Kim’s name was reported on March 3, 2020. Since then, more than 80 statements have been issued, and they have become a routine instrument of North Korean external communication.

Kim Yo Jong’s statements first came to international prominence with the bombing of the inter-Korean liaison office in June 2020. A June 13 statement that month announced in advance that the office would be destroyed, and the act followed three days later. The episode made clear that her statements could translate directly into concrete action.

This year, the frequency of statements has increased. The August 5 statement directed at Japan accused Tokyo of pursuing the capacity for pre-emptive strikes and announced that North Korea would add “clear military options” as countermeasures. The statements targeting the IAEA on September 17 and 19 asserted that North Korea’s status as a nuclear-armed state is unshakeable. Even matters that would previously have been addressed by North Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs or Ministry of National Defense are now being covered by Kim’s statements.

The statements display an interesting variation in register, depending on the audience. Criticism of the United States is frequent, yet direct condemnation of U.S. President Donald Trump by name has been consistently avoided, and the language remains restrained. This likely signals that North Korea has not foreclosed the option of resuming negotiations with Washington.

By contrast, statements directed at South Korea are marked by emotionally charged language. Following a landmine explosion incident on September 21 in the demilitarized zone that left three South Korean soldiers injured — an incident that the South Korean military and the United Nations Command (UNC) attributed to North Korean mines — Kim’s September 29 statement dismissed the account as a “staged farce.” A statement on October 2 went further, expressing visceral revulsion: “The mere thought of that group called South Korea makes my flesh crawl.”

The October 8 statement was a reaction to the South Korean government’s announcement that it had obtained a UN sanctions exemption for a plan to provide medical equipment to North Korea. Kim framed both the South Korean account of the landmine incident and the offer of medical assistance as elements of a single “farce,” and resorted to crude abuse, calling South Korea’s leadership “congenital idiots beyond all reform.” It is a flat-out rejection of what North Korea perceives as South Korea’s condescending attitude.

The following day, October 9, Kim issued “an assessment and position of the Government of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea” on these matters, an unusual format in which a party Central Committee department director was explicitly presenting an official government position.

Behind all this lies Kim Yo Jong’s singular political standing. She became Director of General Affairs at the 9th Congress of the Workers’ Party of Korea in February of this year, but the political authority of her statements derives less from that formal title than from the fact that she is Kim Jong Un’s younger sister. Were Kim Jong Un himself to speak, his words would be received as the supreme leader’s direct will; with Kim Yo Jong as the speaker, strong warnings can be issued while preserving Kim Jong Un’s own policy options.

This normalization of external communication paradoxically creates a problem, what might be called “the inflation of Kim Yo Jong statements.” There was a time when the mere fact that Kim Yo Jong was speaking carried special significance. As statements are deployed across a widening range of topics, that rarity diminishes. The repeated use of confrontational language may also erode the warning value of any individual statement.

That said, it would be premature to equate the inflation of statements with a decline in political significance. There is always the possibility that genuine signals of policy change or military action could be embedded among the frequent outpourings. The bombing of the inter-Korean liaison office serves as precedent: not every statement can be dismissed as bluster.

Nor should we overlook the fact that North Korea, while declaring it will “ignore” South Korea, continues to react repeatedly to South Korean statements and actions. North Korea may be emphasizing a severing of ties with the South, but that does not mean it can afford to disregard South Korea’s military capabilities. There is also a possibility that North Korea is drawing political lines in advance — establishing the conditions under which it would engage with South Korea — in preparation for whatever changes may come in U.S.-North Korea relations.

For Japan, the United States, and South Korea, it is becoming increasingly important to read Kim Yo Jong’s statements carefully. What matters is not just the tone and language, but the ability to distinguish: Is this statement issued on someone’s “authorization”? Is it a repetition of established positions? Or is it a warning of new countermeasures? As the frequency of statements rises, it is vital that genuinely significant warnings do not go unrecognized.
